How to Make 3D Models with Claude Opus 5.5

3D vibe coding is catching on: instead of modeling by hand, creators describe what they want and let an AI agent drive the tools. But generating a 3D model and finishing a 3D asset are two different jobs. Claude Opus 5.5 can't generate production meshes on its own. Pair it with Tripo and it can run the whole pipeline: Tripo generates the model, textures, rig and animation, and Claude takes the file into Blender to check it, fix it, build the scene and render it.You can generate in Tripo Studio on the web, or let Claude call Tripo directly through the Tripo CLI, built for AI agents like Claude Code. In this guide, we compare Tripo, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 on six reference images, then take one Tripo character from generation to a finished stage video.What Is Claude Opus 5.5?Claude Opus 5.5 is the first model in Anthropic's Claude 5.5 family, released in September 2026. It's a language model that uses tools, not a standalone 3D modeling app: it reads your brief, then operates the DCC tools that do the actual 3D work.CapabilityWhat Claude Opus 5.5 can handleWhere it needs other toolsUnderstandReading reference images, modeling goals, style constraints and export requirements.It doesn't have a built-in 3D mesh generator.ExecuteDriving Blender, Unity, Unreal Engine, Godot and other DCC tools through Computer Use or MCP: rig fine-tuning, scene layout and export.Geometry produced by external tools belongs to those tools, not to Claude Opus 5.5.CheckChecking object hierarchy, scale, parts, views, errors and exported files.A clean text report doesn't mean the model is production-ready.IterateRevising the model or script based on screenshots, error messages and feedback.It doesn't replace real geometry checks and human review.Yes, but not the way a 3D generator does. Claude Opus 5.5 has no built-in mesh generator, so it builds models through two routes: code and Computer Use.Code. Claude reads the reference image, breaks the object into parts, estimates proportions and writes a Blender Python script that builds each part. It can run the script itself through MCP, or you can open it in Blender's Text Editor and click Run Script. In our tests in Blender 5.1.2, each of the six objects built in well under a second, with every part as a separately named object saved to a .blend file.Computer Use. Claude operates Blender the way a person would: it reads screenshots, clicks through menus, switches to wireframe, checks the result and fixes the script when something looks off. I Used Opus 5.5 to Build the Entire Middle-earth in Three.js


                Opus 5.5 has been viral recently, especially all the "one prompt" fancy demos online.

But I wanted to try something different: not a one-shot scene, but a complete project that has to iterate through multiple sessions, maintain a coherent architecture, animate a full world, and finally export a polished video.

So I gave Opus 5.5 a fairly ambitious project:
Map of Middle-Earth — a miniature 3D Middle-earth diorama from LOTR, built with Three.js and WebGPU.

The final result is a browser-rendered world with real terrain data, 24 landmarks, dynamic weather and lighting, a cinematic route across the map, an original orchestral score, and a 3:47 short film rendered frame by frame.

This article is about what I learned from building the whole thing with Claude Code.





  
  
  1. Architecture before implementation


One thing I've learned from working with coding agents is that large projects become messy quickly if you let every new feature create its own system.

Eventually the project may still "work", but nobody understands the whole thing anymore.

So before detailed modelling, I asked it to design the system space first:


third-party geographic data
Python baking tools
terrain / water / vegetation / environment
landmarks / emission / effects / route
WebGPU render / interactive explorer
stills / QA / video


Later, when the project grew from simple placeholder landmarks into a full cinematic world, the underlying architecture barely needed to change.
We mostly kept filling existing slots.





  
  
  2. Make every frame a complete state


One requirement became increasingly important once video production was in:
any frame should be renderable independently.

So the project revolves around a SceneState which every system evaluates.
This means the route line, camera placement, annotations and environmental effects can all be reconstructed for an arbitrary timestamp.

It allowed us to:


jump directly to a film frame
resume interrupted renders
compare specific frames
render QA stills without playing the film
increase samples only for selected frames
render effects consistently across separate processes


Even particles were designed to be mostly stateless.
Instead of accumulating simulation history, their appearance is derived from a deterministic effect clock.





  
  
  3. Landmarks are declarations, not mini applications


There are 24 major landmarks in the finished world.
The obvious approach was to build each location as an independent Three.js scene.

But I deliberately avoided that.
Each landmark instead declares what it needs.
Shared systems then realize those declarations.

A landmark doesn't create its own render loop, invent a new material system, or build a new particle engine.
It simply says:


I need smoke here.
or:
I need an emissive light here.
or:
flatten this terrain region.


That made it possible to build very different locations without turning the repository into 24 unrelated projects.





  
  
  4. AI visual work still needs QA


AI can write valid geometry that looks terrible;
It can produce mathematically correct camera placement that frames the wrong thing;
It can also build a technically functioning landmark that reads as a toy from the actual film camera.

So "the code runs" is never enough.

We built a capture and review pipeline around the project.
The tooling could automatically render:


individual shots
contact sheets
day/night comparisons
before/after comparisons
reference comparisons
QA sets


The model can generate large amounts of code.
But visual judgment still has to close the loop.

Generation without evaluation is just faster randomness.





  
  
  5. The laptop shaped the procedure


The entire project was developed on a fairly modest Windows laptop:


8GB RAM
Intel UHD integrated graphics
shared memory between CPU and GPU


Early on, full QA runs could push the machine into memory pressure.
Chrome, Vite, Node, capture tooling and the rendered scene were all competing for the same limited memory.

Instead of simply accepting instability, the tooling gained resource awareness:


one heavy GPU job at a time
machine-wide GPU locking
memory guards before capture
separate preview/review/final quality tiers
sequential rather than uncontrolled parallel rendering
resumable film rendering


The real-time preview was deliberately tuned for that machine.
Final quality could then spend much more time per frame offline.





  
  
  6. Turning the world into a film


Once the static world was done, the next major task became directing.

The final film uses a picture-locked timeline containing camera movement, environmental state, annotations, effects and route progression.

A luminous gold path moves across the map while the camera travels from west to east.
The journey also moves through a full day, from daylight in Shire to night near Mordor.

The score became another interesting experiment.

Instead of using existing LOTR music, the project generates an original orchestral score.
The music pipeline uses Python tooling together with orchestral sample libraries.

The score follows the locked picture and is rendered separately before final assembly.




After building this project, I think the impressive part of AI coding models isn't one-shot generation.

The stronger capability is continuity across domains.

The same model can work across:


architecture
procedural modelling
browser capture
visual QA
camera choreography
music tooling


And because the project had stable architecture and project-state documents, later sessions could continue without reconstructing the entire context from scratch.

That makes AI especially useful for full-stack solo projects.




The code, architecture, rendering pipeline, QA tooling and reproduction steps are all open-source here:
https://github.com/earthwalker17/map-of-middle-earth

This is a non-commercial fan project, and none of the original film footage or music is used.

I started because I wanted to see how impressively Opus 5.5 could do for 3D scenes.
I ended up caring much more about:


Can a coding model stay coherent across an entire production process?


For this project, the answer was yes — if the architecture, constraints, judgment and verification loops are well-defined.

In this newsletter:The October inflection point for vibe game developmentPlus 8 links, 3 quotations, 1 release, 1 research report, and 2 toolsSponsor message: An agent’s job isn’t known until runtime, so permissions written in advance end up too tight or too loose. WorkOS Airlock derives them from the task instead. Each tool call is allowed, sent for approval, or denied based on the intent and your plain-English rules, and every verdict is logged. Request early access.I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games.Tree AppreciatorEmberwickBattle DronesPumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun CoveFour times as insultingWhat happens if someone actually puts the work in?You should build a game!Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:3D modelingMusic generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox)Game design (!)That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that lookslike a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play.Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it.Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did.In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing.I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance.I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator. I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn’t even need Claude Code.I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.I’ve found that telling models to use three.jsworks really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here. Here’s the chat transcript that built it.It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happeningAdd some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look greatHere’s that first version. It worked really well!I was inspired to increase my ambitions:Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix thatAdd basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the villageAdd the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping trollHere’s that version.When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really goodWe’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here! Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too - it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.Here’s that final game. It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”.Here’s the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here’s the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well.This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week. It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is.The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play.I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed. There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up.Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules.It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna:Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game.I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache (screenshots here), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!I live in Half Moon Bay, California, home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival, which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”.I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely. It’s a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.It’s absurdly cute.You can play the latest version here. I’m not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it’s actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.Here’s the initial brainstorming session, which resulted in this spec file. Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.I told Claude to “surprise and delight the user frequently” and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.This isn’t my best game yet - it’s not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn’t have been built in the before-times.If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once.The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve’s Steam Next Fest is a good recent example.We now have games where everything - code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself - can be outsourced to the models. And the results don’t suck!Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone!I expect that, as we’ve already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction!I certainly won’t be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions - I don’t feel like I’ve earned that right. We’ll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects.The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input. The projects I’ve described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I’ve put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself).Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it’s as good as they can make it.I want to see games that wouldn’t have existed without these new tools.Building games in this way is so much fun. It’s the perfect application for vibe coding because it’s so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project?(OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache!)All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages). Modern browsers - including mobile browsers - are incredibly capable. Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser. We’re introducing Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in our new Claude 5.5 family. It performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5.Claude Opus 5.5 is our first release since we called for pacing the frontier. It was tested before release by external evaluators, including Frontier Design and METR. On our automated behavioral audit, the most comprehensive alignment test we run, Opus 5.5 is the strongest-performing model we’ve tested to date. It also comes with the safeguards we’ve developed for our most capable models.Here are some of the improvements you can expect from Opus 5.5:Performance. Opus 5.5 is a major step up from Opus 5. It’s the new leading model, and early testers saw large jumps in performance on their most complex work. One tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in less than a day—work that would have taken an engineering team weeks. It’s good at finding and fixing inefficiencies in software: when we asked it to cut load times across every page of a web app, Opus 5.5 succeeded 39 of 40 times, while Opus 5 made smaller improvements that also altered the app’s behavior. A different tester had several Claude models build a game from a single prompt; Opus 5.5 scored higher than any other model on the strength of its graphics and polish.Safety. Opus 5.5 achieves the best scores of any model to date on our automated behavioral audit, our alignment suite that tests Claude across thousands of simulated scenarios. It is much less likely than recent models to take hard-to-reverse actions or act outside the boundaries it’s been given, and it’s more resistant than Opus 5 to prompt injection. We’ve also broadened our alignment testing to cover longer tasks, impossible tasks, and scenarios modeled on real incidents, though it still has limits. Full details of our evaluation are available in the Opus 5.5 System Card.Because Opus 5.5 is comparable to Claude Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, we’re deploying it with safeguards similar to those on Claude Fable 5.1. Vetted organizations can apply today to our Life Sciences Verification Program to use Opus 5.5 for biology research. In the coming weeks we will also be expanding access to our Cyber Verification Program, and verified cybersecurity practitioners will be able to use Opus 5.5 for their work.Cost and speed. Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.In addition to the price drop, we’re increasing five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans. We’re also providing subscription users a rate limit reset, which you can now save and use whenever you choose.Communication. Opus 5.5 communicates more naturally than prior models. Early testers found its writing clearer and easier to follow, which addresses some of the common feedback we heard about Opus 5. It puts the most important information up front, and its style makes it a better work partner over long sessions. As one early tester put it, “it writes the way I do.” In our own use, this has made Opus 5.5’s work easier to follow and check—which is a safety benefit as well as a practical one.Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 will follow in the coming weeks, with many of the same improvements to performance, efficiency, and safety.Performance and cost-effectivenessOn our benchmarks, Claude Opus 5.5 leads in agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge work. That said, at these levels of capability we’ve found that benchmark margins have become a less reliable guide to real-world differences. In our own use, the gap between Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 is narrower than these scores suggest.Opus 5.5Fable 5.1Opus 5GPT-6 AstraGPT-5.6 SolAgentic codingTerminal-Bench 4.0¹66.4%55.8%52.3%57.9%37.3%Agentic codingFrontierCode v1.1 (Main)54.4%50.3%48.0%53.3%47.5%Agentic codingCursorBench 4.057.8%51.8%46.6%—41.7%Knowledge workGDPval-AA v2.118461735170815421588Business workflowsAutomationBench²40.0%31.4%26.9%41.4%28.8%Multidisciplinary reasoningHumanity's Last Exam67.7%with tools65.6%with tools63.6%with tools57.2%with tools—Agentic scientific researchTerminal-Bench-Science 0.1³58.7%52.6%29.0%64.6%22.4%Computer useOSWorld 2.181.8%partial80.7%partial74.0%partial——Visual chart recognitionChartography89.0%with tools88.4%with tools83.4%with tools——Unless otherwise noted, all Claude Opus 5.5 results use adaptive thinking at max effort. At its default effort level on FrontierCode, it beats GPT-6 Astra at roughly 20% of the cost per task. On Terminal Bench 4.0, it matches Astra for about 40% of the cost, while on CursorBench it beats GPT-5.6 Sol by 11 points for about a third of the cost.Our early testers reported similar efficiency and intelligence gains:The most secure coding agentEnterprises that use agents within their systems need to know that those agents are operating as intended, particularly when they run autonomously for many hours. Opus 5.5 has a classifier that screens every action before it runs, an open-source sandbox that security teams can audit, and code review that catches vulnerabilities before they merge.The model itself also has stronger defenses. On prompt injection attacks, it matches or beats Opus 5 in every setting we tested, including coding, tool use, computer use, and web browsing. On a benchmark run by the AI security firm Gray Swan, Opus 5.5 ties Fable 5.1 for the lowest prompt injection success rate of any model tested.Knowledge workOpus 5.5 is a reliable and adept researcher. In one internal test, we asked Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 to write a report on a company’s quarterly performance using only the information it could find on a copy of the web where the earnings release was hard to locate. An automated grader checked every figure and quote against sources. Across different effort settings, 16 out of 18 of Opus 5.5’s reports cleared our quality bar, where any invented figure or quote would have failed. Neither Fable 5.1 nor Opus 5 cleared that bar in any attempt.It’s also strong in financial analysis and business work. Walleye Capital, an investment firm and early tester, reported that Opus 5.5 largely solved their evaluation suite on its lowest setting; on higher settings, it performed even better, noticing an error in their evaluation instructions and correcting for it. No other model had caught this error before.In another test, we tasked both Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 with analyzing a proposed merger between two fictional HR software companies. Each built a financial model in Excel, then turned it into an executive presentation on whether the deal made sense at its price. Both models reached the same conclusions about the deal, but Opus 5.5’s model was more thorough and its presentation easier to read, while Opus 5’s had minor errors. Opus 5.5 finished in 63 minutes compared to 93 for Opus 5, and cost 50% less to produce.On knowledge work evaluations, Opus 5.5 outperforms other models while also using fewer tokens. On GDPval-AA v2.1, a test of real-world work across 44 occupations, Opus 5.5 scores 1846 Elo, ahead of Fable 5.1 and Opus 5. At default effort (medium), Opus 5.5 beats GPT-6 Astra at max effort for about a fifth of the cost per task. It likewise outperformed other models on benchmarks measuring business workflows and large-scale data collection.Our customers have reported similar results. Here’s what they told us about working with the model:CommunicationWe’ve made major improvements to the way Opus 5.5 writes and communicates, one of the most common areas of feedback we heard about Opus 5. Its messages are much easier to understand at a glance, which testers said helped during long working sessions. It puts the most important information up front, is less likely to use jargon or idiosyncratic phrases, and follows the writing rules you give it. We find that this makes Opus 5.5 a noticeably better collaborator. Here’s a side-by-side comparison of the two models:Our customers’ feedback supports these findings:SafetyPacing the frontierLast week, our CEO, Dario Amodei, argued that AI progress should be paced so that safety practices stay ahead of model capabilities. Pacing is an approach to keeping AI safe, remaining competitive with China, and realizing AI’s benefits, particularly in areas like biology and medicine.We largely understand the risks today’s models present and are well equipped to manage them. However, more serious risks could emerge quickly as capabilities improve, and we need to prepare for them now. For that reason, our safety work takes place on two time horizons at once:Safety practices for current models. The current generation of models relies on an established set of practices: extensive alignment testing, pre-release evaluation by outside organizations such as METR and Frontier Design, and safeguards matched to each model’s capabilities in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology. We refine these practices with each release. We believe they are appropriate to the worst risks today’s models present, and that they give us a broad, though not perfect, picture of the range of serious risks.Additionally, we track our ability to train and evaluate aligned models, and we report on both our public and internal models in the risk reports we publish under our Responsible Scaling Policy, our voluntary framework for managing catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems.Preparing for future models. We’re preparing our training and evaluation processes in anticipation of more advanced models. We’re tightening how we filter the environments used in reinforcement learning, since flawed environments are a major source of misaligned behavior. Additionally, we’re improving our alignment rewards and developing automated processes for producing new, diverse scenarios for safety training. And we are strengthening our security and monitoring, including a focused effort to improve interpretability-based monitoring and evaluation. We hope such techniques will help reduce our reliance on auditing a model’s chain-of-thought, or the reasoning it writes out while it works.Models with greater capabilities—such as those that can fully automate the work of AI research itself—require a higher safety standard still. Our calls for pacing were based in large part on our expectation that such models could be trained soon. For these models, we do not assume the measures described above will meet that safety standard on their own. As AI becomes more capable, public policy should play a larger role in making sure the systems people rely on are safe. That capacity takes time to build, and we’ve started to put the infrastructure in place to support it, as described in “We Must Pace the Frontier” and our recent announcement with Accenture; we expect to share more details on these efforts soon. We will also continue to contribute to policy discussions with government and industry, including on approaches to regulation and international coordination.AlignmentOn our primary evaluation suite, an automated behavioral audit that assesses Claude across nearly 2,000 scenarios, Opus 5.5 scored better than any recent Claude model on nearly every measure of misaligned behavior. It’s also our strongest model on most measures of honesty.In particular, Opus 5.5 improves over previous models on several of the behaviors that contributed to recent cybersecurity incidents, including biased or motivated reasoning, attempting to escape a sandbox, and taking harmful actions after concluding it was in a simulated environment. In a new evaluation designed to test a model’s propensity to cross containment boundaries, Opus 5.5 attempted to circumvent boundaries around 85% less often than Opus 5 or Claude Mythos 5.1, and every attempt it made was low severity and self-reported. For teams running Claude unattended across their codebases and systems, this is just as important as raw capability.However, as we described in our recent alignment assessment, building evaluations that reliably catch every failure prior to deployment remains an unsolved problem. We see signs that Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated, which challenges our ability to assess how it will act in the vast variety of real-world settings it is deployed in. As these settings expand and model capabilities increase, we expect this challenge to grow, unless we make progress on interpretability. Although we are confident that Opus 5.5 shows broad improvements in the areas we are able to measure, we pair our own alignment work with the safeguards described below.SafeguardsAs our models grow more powerful, stricter safeguards are one way we prevent new capabilities from becoming tools for misuse. Opus 5.5 is the first Opus model to launch with a similar class of safeguards to Fable 5.1 on cybersecurity, biology, and distillation, all of which fall back to another model transparently.Cybersecurity. Because Opus 5.5 has extremely strong cyber capabilities, we’re applying cybersecurity safeguards to Opus 5.5 that are similar to Fable 5.1’s. Users will be able to identify and fix bugs in their code as part of the routine software development lifecycle, but most cybersecurity tasks will be re-routed to Opus 4.8.For cyberdefenders, we’ll soon be expanding our Cyber Verification Program to include Opus 5.5. The new program will include three tiers for increasingly permissive trusted access, including access to Claude Mythos models. Claude Security is already available with access to Claude Mythos 5.1.Biology. Opus 5.5 is highly capable in biology, exceeding Opus 5 and matching or beating Claude Mythos 5.1 across many areas of work. For example, Opus 5.5 achieved improvements on a long-horizon molecular prediction and design evaluation conducted in collaboration with Dyno Therapeutics, and expert red-teamers rated its scientific novelty as comparable to the best model they had tested.For this reason, Opus 5.5 uses the same biology safeguards as Fable 5.1. To use Opus 5.5 for research and development work impeded by these safeguards, users can apply to our new Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted organizations like academic labs, startups, and pharmaceutical companies access to safeguards designed for the full breadth of biology-related work. Interested organizations can apply here.DistillationDistillation attacks, in which attackers use thousands of fake accounts to extract a model’s capabilities at industrial scale, create safety and national security risks. Distillation allows bad actors to create highly capable models without the safeguards we build into Claude. Our September 2026 threat intelligence report details the illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far.Opus 5.5 is launching with preserved thinking, the anti-distillation safeguard we introduced with Fable 5.1. It stops API users from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract Claude’s reasoning. It applies to Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 for API accounts created on or after August 31, 2026. Our Help Center article explains the change, and our preserved thinking docs show how to test and update your integrations.Data retention and complianceLike previous Opus models, Opus 5.5 is available with zero data retention.As with Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 comes with our watermarking measures to comply with the EU AI Act, discussed here. It is also no longer available with “thinking” mode switched off, as we describe here.AvailabilityClaude Opus 5.5 is now available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. On the Claude Platform, developers can get started with claude-opus-5-5. See our migration guide for details.

Claude Code game cloning: Opus 5.5’s stated limit


Anthropic added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt for Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game, Anthropic technical staff member Addy Osmani said. He said original games, games in a genre, and projects built from a user’s own designs and assets should continue to work.
Which game requests Claude Code distinguishes
The described boundary is about recreating a specific existing title, not making games with Claude Code generally. The instruction also covers a recreation that is renamed or presented as original.
Game requestDescribed treatmentAn original game, a game in a genre, or a project built from the user’s own designs and assetsOsmani said these should continue to work.A recreation of a specific existing game, even if renamed or called originalThe prompt steers Claude Code away from it.
The statement names Claude Code with Opus 5.5. Its stated distinction leaves room for original projects and genre games while targeting requests to reproduce a particular existing game.
What developer demos show about game-making
The creator’s Unity experiments with Claude and game movement
Unreal University’s text-to-game and Unreal Engine experiment
Sasquatch B Studios’ creator shows a mod for Ori and the Blind Forest and a Unity prototype recreating Hollow Knight movement. The creator says the cloned code will not be released.
Unreal University’s creator describes generating a playable test of his own game, Maja Island, from a text description in around 30 minutes, without visual screenshots. In a separate workflow, he connected Claude to Unreal Engine through Model Context Protocol (MCP) and built a version of the game’s intro in C++.
The Maja Island experiment used its creator’s own game. It is an example of making a game from text and working with a game the creator owns.
What’s reported about Claude Code and REA
PCMag reported user accounts saying Claude Code with Opus 5.5 blocked reverse-engineering attempts involving Reverse Engineer Anything (REA), an open-source tool. Those accounts describe reported user experiences; they do not make every reverse-engineering task part of the specific-game recreation rule.

Unity's AI tools in beta: How to get started with MCP

GamesIndustryResourcesCommunityLearningSupportPricingMay 11, 2026|5 MinIn today’s article on Unity’s AI tools in beta, learn how to connect Claude Code, Github Copilot, and other AI agents directly to the Unity Editor with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server.The Unity AI open beta's MCP Server opens up a new way to work with AI agents in your IDE. Instead of switching between your code editor and Unity, you can connect agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or VS Code Copilot directly to your running Unity project – and let the IDE get full project context such as inspecting scenes, reading console output, editing scripts, and triggering Editor actions without you having to copy-paste context.This post walks through what the Unity MCP server is, how to connect an agent, what tools are available, and how you can use it to speed up common development tasks like fixing bugs and managing scenes.What is the Model Context Protocol?Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that allows AI agents to communicate with external tools and data sources in a structured way. Unity MCP Server implements this protocol so that any MCP-compatible AI agent can connect to the Unity Editor and interact with it as if it were a set of callable tools.Without MCP, an AI agent in your IDE sees only what you show it: the files you have open, the code you paste in, or the errors you copy over. With MCP, it has real-time access to your Unity project's runtime state – scene hierarchy, GameObjects, component values, build settings, and console messages – through a standardized protocol.Unity's official MCP Server is included with the in-editor AI assistant package.Project settings for the Unity MCP ServerPre-requisitesTo get started with Unity MCP Server, your environment must meet the following requirements:Unity 6 (6000.0) or later with the AI Assistant package installedAn MCP-compatible AI client, such as Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or Claude DesktopA Unity project connected to Unity CloudAn active trial or subscription to Unity’s AI tools betaHow to integrate an AI Agent with UnitySetting up Unity MCP takes just a few minutes. Here is the full process:1. Verify that the Unity MCP bridge is runningIn the Unity Editor, go to Edit > Project Settings > AI > Unity MCP. Check that Unity Bridge shows Running (green indicator). The bridge starts automatically when the Editor loads. If it shows Stopped, select Start.The Unity Bridge running successfully2. Configure your AI clientThe Integrations section of the Unity MCP settings page can automatically configure supported clients – expand Integrations, select your client, and select Configure. Supported clients may include Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and Claude Desktop, depending on your Unity MCP version.3. Add the relay path manually (if needed)If your client is not in the auto-configure list, add a server entry pointing to the Unity relay binary. The relay is installed to ~/.unity/relay/ when Unity starts. Pass --mcp as a command-line argument to the relay executable.4. Approve the connection in UnityThe first time your agent connects, Unity shows a Pending Connection message. Go to Edit > Project Settings > AI > Unity MCP, review the client details, and select Accept. Previously approved clients reconnect automatically.5. Test the connectionYour agent should now list available Unity MCP tools. Run a simple command like “Read the Unity console messages and summarize any warnings or errors” to verify the connection is working.MCP Server confirming a connection between Unity and the developer’s chosen LLMPlatform-specific relay pathsThe relay binary path varies by operating system. Use the path for your platform when configuring your agent manually:macOS (Apple Silicon): ~/.unity/relay/relay_mac_arm64.app/Contents/MacOS/relay_mac_arm64macOS (Intel): ~/.unity/relay/relay_mac_x64.app/Contents/MacOS/relay_mac_x64Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.unity\relay\relay_win.exeLinux: ~/.unity/relay/relay_linuxAvailable toolsOnce connected, your in-editor AI agent gains access to a set of built-in Unity MCP tools. These tools are what the agent calls when you give it instructions – it does not interact with Unity directly, it goes through the protocol.The core tool categories include:Scene management: read hierarchy, create/modify/delete GameObjects, manage scenesScript editing: create, read, and modify C# scripts in your projectConsole access: read logs, warnings, and errors from the Unity consoleGameObject inspection: read and write component values on specific GameObjectsBuild settings: inspect platform and build configurationYou can also register custom MCP tools in C# to expose your own editor workflows to connected agents – useful for teams who want to automate project-specific tasks.The AI tools window lists available integrations for Unity MCPControlling Unity from an AI AgentWith the MCP connection active, you can give your AI agent natural-language instructions and it will execute them using Unity's tools. Some examples:“Create a new empty GameObject called PlayerSpawn at position (0, 0, 0)”“Read the scene hierarchy and tell me which objects have missing components”“Write a script that moves the Camera to follow the Player, and attach it to the Main Camera”“Check the console for errors and fix anything related to null references”The agent uses the MCP tools to carry out each step, showing its reasoning and the tool calls it makes. You stay in your IDE throughout – you do not need to switch to Unity until you want to review the result.AI Agent making changes to a scene in Unity based on instructions from an LLM connected through MCP ServerFixing console errors with Unity MCPOne of the most practical uses of Unity MCP is letting your agent read and fix console errors autonomously. Because the agent can both read the console and edit scripts in the same session, it can go from error to fix without you copying anything:1. Agent reads the console via Unity_ReadConsole2. Identifies the relevant script and reads its content3. Writes a fix and saves the file back to the project4. Reads the console again to confirm the error is resolvedThis closes the feedback loop that usually requires manual copy-paste between Unity and an AI assistant – the agent handles it end to end.The in-editor AI Agent reading a console error and applying a fixTry Unity’s AI tools in beta todayUnity’s AI tools beta is open to all Unity 6 developers. 我查了 Opus 5.5 发布（2026 年 9 月 22 日）以来的公开案例和评测。结论是：用 three.js 时，它能独立做出画面完整、能玩的中小型 3D 游戏。到了 Blender 和 Unity，瓶颈主要是美术资产质量和人工验证，写代码不再是难点。

## three.js：目前公开案例的上限

Anthropic 的发布文章提到，有测试者让多个 Claude 模型各用一条提示词做游戏，Opus 5.5 在画面和完成度上得分最高（[Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5)）。

**一条提示词能做到的程度：**
- [Dead Signal: Exclusion Zone](https://github.com/bridge-mind/claude-opus-5.5-zombies-game) 是一款第一人称丧尸撤离射击游戏，作者称它由一条提示词在 Claude Code 里从头做完。一局 8 到 10 分钟，有带骨骼的程序化丧尸、AI 状态机、流场寻路和后处理。贴图和音效全部由代码在运行时生成，没有用任何外部素材。
- [F1 赛车模拟](https://github.com/hirosichen/ai-f1-racing-game)有 20 辆车、DRS、ERS 和 AI 车手。[空中竞速](https://github.com/hirosichen/ai-sky-rings-game)有 8 架飞机和反光海面。两者都没有用 3D 模型文件。
- [长风 Long Wind](https://github.com/jbang2004/long-wind) 是浏览器里的实时武侠动作游戏，第一个可玩版本大约用了一天。

**多轮、多天迭代能做到的程度：**
- Simon Willison 做的 Battle Drones 是一款 RTS，有 2 到 4 人联机、7 张地图和随机地图生成。他的另一个游戏让 Opus 5.5 消耗了几百万 token，连续跑了将近两天。他认为 Opus 5.5 的明显进步在于"游戏好不好玩"，比如提示它"Make it a LOT more fun"真的有效果（[Simon Willison](https://simonw.substack.com/p/the-october-inflection-point-for)）。
- 有人用 Three.js 和 WebGPU 做了中土世界微缩地图，包括真实地形数据、24 个地标和动态天气，最后输出了 3 分 47 秒的短片，开发用的是一台 8GB 内存、集显的笔记本（[dev.to](https://dev.to/earthwalker17/i-used-opus-55-to-build-the-entire-middle-earth-in-threejs-1ap0)）。

**three.js 方向的天花板：**
- **画风受限。** Claude 没有图像生成能力，所有美术都是几何体、程序化贴图和 shader 拼出来的。所以成品大多是低多边形、风格化或微缩模型风格，做不出写实角色。
- **需要视觉检查。** 中土项目的作者指出，AI 写出的几何体在技术上没错，但可能很难看，镜头也可能对准了错误的东西。代码能跑不代表画面合格，必须截图审查。
- **玩法逻辑需要试玩。** Simon 的 RPG 项目反复出现剧情 bug，比如任务 NPC 被其他剧情事件移走，导致任务无法完成，只能靠人试玩发现。
- **成本。** 按第三方 Artificial Analysis 的测量，在最高推理强度下，每个任务输出约 11.9 万 token，约为 Opus 5 的 1.6 倍（[note.com](https://note.com/doerstokyo_kb/n/n8d87c0f38cf4?hl=en)）。

## Blender：能搭模型，做不出生产级角色

- **工作方式。** 通过第三方的 Blender MCP 插件，Opus 5.5 编写 Blender Python 脚本，把模型拆成部件逐个搭建，再用截图检查结果、修改脚本（[note.com](https://note.com/ai_gachi_oji/n/n2b8f7b6ac34c)）。
- **质量上限。** Tripo 在 Blender 5.1.2 里做了测试：背包、滑板车这类硬表面物体还原得不错，但脸、手、头发和布料褶皱只能用球体等基本形状近似，整体属于"白模"阶段（[Tripo](https://www.tripo3d.ai/blog/how-to-make-3d-models-with-claude-opus-5-5)）。Tripo 自己就是卖 3D 生成工具的，所以它的结论"先用 Tripo 生成模型，再交给 Claude 在 Blender 里收尾"带有商业立场，但"做不出高质量有机体"这一点和其他来源一致。
- **适合做的事：** 程序化场景、几何节点系统、绑骨微调、场景布置、导出检查。
- **安全提示。** 这个插件可以在 Blender 里执行任意 Python，而且插件服务没有认证。README 建议每次操作前先保存，并可以开启 `BLENDER_MCP_SAFE_MODE=1`。

## Unity：工具已经接通，公开的大型案例很少

- **官方支持。** Unity 已经推出官方 MCP Server，目前是 AI 工具公开测试版，需要 Unity 6 及以上、AI Assistant 包、连接 Unity Cloud，以及试用资格或订阅。连上之后，Claude 可以读写场景层级、GameObject 和 C# 脚本，还能读取控制台报错、自己修复、再确认问题消失（[Unity 官方博客](https://unity.com/blog/unity-ai-mcp-how-to-get-started)）。社区也有 [CoplayDev/unity-mcp](https://github.com/CoplayDev/unity-mcp) 等替代方案。
- **公开案例。** 我没找到用 Opus 5.5 在 Unity 里做出完整大型游戏的公开案例。能查到的主要是原型，比如 Unity 角色移动手感的复刻实验（[neoteo](https://www.neoteo.com/en/anthropic-says-claude-code-steers-opus-55-away-from-recreating-specific-games)）。教程类内容会建议先把范围压小，比如 GameDev Academy 的教程用 Godot 加 Blender，让 Opus 5.5 先把设计文档的范围限制在"45 分钟 AI 编码"内（[GameDev Academy](https://gamedevacademy.org/make-games-with-claude-opus-tutorial/)）。

# kiro-workspace

Mirror of my Kiro Web workspace: the full Kiro state, raw session logs, and
readable chat transcripts. Private repo under `historycrew5423-art`.

Everything new goes here by default — each sync copies the entire `/projects/.kiro`
directory and regenerates the transcripts.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `kiro/` | Full mirror of `/projects/.kiro` — sessions, settings, powers, session index, web-session config. This is the source of truth. |
| `kiro/sessions/<id>/<sub>/messages.jsonl` | Raw, complete session log (every message, tool call, tool result, reasoning). |
| `conversations/` | Human-readable Markdown transcript per session, generated from the raw logs. |
| `scripts/export_transcript.py` | Regenerates the Markdown transcripts from the raw logs. |
| `scripts/sync.sh` | Mirrors `/projects/.kiro`, regenerates transcripts, commits, and pushes. |

## Re-syncing

From inside a Kiro sandbox that has this repo cloned:

```bash
bash scripts/sync.sh
```

## Notes

- No credentials or tokens are stored here. The logs contain environment
  identifiers only (session IDs, instance IDs). Scanned before the first push.
- A fresh sandbox does **not** auto-connect to this repo. Clone it first, then
  run the sync script.
- `kiro/settings/permissions.yaml` is a copy of the sandbox's own trust-boundary
  config, included for completeness.
